The paper is organized as follow: • In Section 2, the related works and the contributions are dis- cussed. • Section 3 describes the proposed approach. • Section 4 presents the experiments, with details on the datasets and the baselines used for the comparisons. • Finally, in Section 5, conclusions are drawn and future works are outlined. 2. Related work The importance of autonomous systems in precision farming has ex- ponentially grown in the last few years (Thayer et al., 2020; Berenstein and Edan, 2018; Williams et al., 2020; Xiong et al., 2020). For the yield estimation task, alongside range sensors ( e.g., LIDAR or lasers), there is increasing adoption of vision-based methods (mostly based on CNNs) that are very effective also in unstructured or partially unstructured environments. A modern vision-based yield estimation approach is a complex system capable to detect, track and map the fruits collecting streams of images. Such a system consists of different functional modules, among which the most relevant is certainly the fruit detection module. Its purpose is to detect and locate the fruits within a single image. In this section, we first provide an overview of the methods used for fruit localization and then we analyze how these methodologies are employed for yield estimation. 2.1. Object detection and counting for agriculture applications Fully supervised CNN architectures for detection and counting have achieved impressive results in a wide variety of datasets and tasks (Zhang et al., 2015, 2017; Khan et al., 2016; Bargoti and Un- derwood, 2017a). Since it is well known that hand-crafted features are not robust to image non-idealities, CNN models, which provide more robust descrip- tors, have become more popular even in agricultural contexts. In Stein et al. (2016) the authors present a yield estimation framework that combines the information from auxiliary sensors and the visual features extracted by a CNN. The proposed strategy is composed of a fruit detector based on FasterRCNN (Ren et al., 2015), a LIDAR sensor and a GPS-RTK coupled with an inertial unit. Fruit matching, occlusions and multi-view errors are avoided by estimating the robot pose and by 3D positioning the detected fruits. Bargoti and Underwood (2017b) presents a solution that combines semantic segmentation maps, com- puted with a CNN architecture and a Multi Layer Perceptron, with GPS data. In the last years, researchers have focused on strategies that rely only on monocular cameras and remove the need for range and differ- ential positioning sensors. Besides the reduction of the costs, this allows extending the applicability of those systems also in indoor scenarios. Following this direction, Nellithimaru and Kantor (2019) uses only RGB images collected by a UGV for yield estimation within grape orchards. The authors take advantage of MaskRCNN (He et al., 2017) to perform fruit segmentation. Redundant counts and occlusions are avoided by localizing the robot pose and the fruit locations with a vision-based SLAM method. Multiple-counting errors can be avoided also using Structure-from-Motion, as in Liu et al. (2018, 2019). To per- form yield estimation in a mango orchard, the former uses a semantic segmentation CNN while the latter relies on an object detector one. In both cases, occlusions and redundant counts are avoided by combining a Kalman-based object tracker with a semantic Structure-from-Motion algorithm. More recently, other approaches try also to perform yield estimation with hyperspectral images, such as in Gutiérrez et al. (2019), where this sensor is used to estimate the yield in large mango orchards. 2.3.

Since, in this case, the optimization is not supervised with quantities that explicitly measure the desired output variable, it is common to exploit coherency losses or auxiliary tasks. In this case, weak supervision information ( i.e., pres- ence/absence labels) is first used to train a simple presence/absence classifier, whose goal is to predict whether the input image contains fruits or not. Introduction In the last few years, autonomous systems have become increasingly pervasive in agricultural applications. Their use has brought several benefits and allowed the growers to (i) enhance monitoring and control of their cultivation, (ii) optimize the yield operations and ease the maintenance procedures and (iii) save resources and minimize human efforts (Zermas et al., 2020; Sulistyo et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2011; Lambert et al., 2014; Tong et al., 2021; de Araújo et al., 2015). Among the different key operations in agricultural scenarios, yield estimation, whose objective is to measure the total yield of a given crop is certainly one of those that benefited the most from these solutions. Their advan- tages are particularly evident in contexts with very wide cultivations or in scenarios where human intervention is limited or completely prohibited (e.g., during the current COVID-19 pandemic outbreak). Most of the State-of-the-Art (SotA) yield estimation systems employ robotic platforms mainly equipped with three types of sensors: range sensors (e.g., LIDAR and sonar sensors), localization sensors ( e.g., GPS and GPS-RTK) and vision systems ( e.g., monocular, multi-spectral and stereo cameras). ∗ Corresponding author. Since it is well known that hand-crafted features are not robust to image non-idealities, CNN models, which provide more robust descrip- tors, have become more popular even in agricultural contexts. In Stein et al. (2016) the authors present a yield estimation framework that combines the information from auxiliary sensors and the visual features extracted by a CNN. The proposed strategy is composed of a fruit detector based on FasterRCNN (Ren et al., 2015), a LIDAR sensor and a GPS-RTK coupled with an inertial unit. Fruit matching, occlusions and multi-view errors are avoided by estimating the robot pose and by 3D positioning the detected fruits. Bargoti and Underwood (2017b) presents a solution that combines semantic segmentation maps, com- puted with a CNN architecture and a Multi Layer Perceptron, with GPS data. In the last years, researchers have focused on strategies that rely only on monocular cameras and remove the need for range and differ- ential positioning sensors. Besides the reduction of the costs, this allows extending the applicability of those systems also in indoor scenarios. Following this direction, Nellithimaru and Kantor (2019) uses only RGB images collected by a UGV for yield estimation within grape orchards. The authors take advantage of MaskRCNN (He et al., 2017) to perform fruit segmentation. Redundant counts and occlusions are avoided by localizing the robot pose and the fruit locations with a vision-based SLAM method. Multiple-counting errors can be avoided also using Structure-from-Motion, as in Liu et al. (2018, 2019). To per- form yield estimation in a mango orchard, the former uses a semantic segmentation CNN while the latter relies on an object detector one. In both cases, occlusions and redundant counts are avoided by combining a Kalman-based object tracker with a semantic Structure-from-Motion algorithm. More recently, other approaches try also to perform yield estimation with hyperspectral images, such as in Gutiérrez et al. Related work The importance of autonomous systems in precision farming has ex- ponentially grown in the last few years (Thayer et al., 2020; Berenstein and Edan, 2018; Williams et al., 2020; Xiong et al., 2020). For the yield estimation task, alongside range sensors ( e.g., LIDAR or lasers), there is increasing adoption of vision-based methods (mostly based on CNNs) that are very effective also in unstructured or partially unstructured environments. A modern vision-based yield estimation approach is a complex system capable to detect, track and map the fruits collecting streams of images. Such a system consists of different functional modules, among which the most relevant is certainly the fruit detection module. Its purpose is to detect and locate the fruits within a single image. The proposed strategy is composed of a fruit detector based on FasterRCNN (Ren et al., 2015), a LIDAR sensor and a GPS-RTK coupled with an inertial unit. Fruit matching, occlusions and multi-view errors are avoided by estimating the robot pose and by 3D positioning the detected fruits. Bargoti and Underwood (2017b) presents a solution that combines semantic segmentation maps, com- puted with a CNN architecture and a Multi Layer Perceptron, with GPS data. In the last years, researchers have focused on strategies that rely only on monocular cameras and remove the need for range and differ- ential positioning sensors. Besides the reduction of the costs, this allows extending the applicability of those systems also in indoor scenarios. Following this direction, Nellithimaru and Kantor (2019) uses only RGB images collected by a UGV for yield estimation within grape orchards. The authors take advantage of MaskRCNN (He et al., 2017) to perform fruit segmentation. In both cases, occlusions and redundant counts are avoided by combining a Kalman-based object tracker with a semantic Structure-from-Motion algorithm.
